I am 73 years old, and I have worked this same 4.1 mu of land in Quzhou for 50 years. My bones know the soil better than any book. With only my wife and me in the household, I cannot afford heavy labor or risky experiments, so I stick to the wheat-maize rotation that has always put food on our table.

For winter wheat, I will sow my usual improved variety in mid-October, right after the summer maize comes off. I will spread compound fertilizer at sowing and topdress with urea at jointing in spring — about 16 kg of nitrogen per mu in total, plus phosphorus and potassium. My well gives me water when I need it, so I will irrigate three times: once at sowing if the autumn is dry, once before winter to protect the seedlings from freezing, and once at jointing when the wheat wakes up hungry. I will spray twice for aphids and rust, because they come every year without fail. I will run the rotary tiller after the maize harvest to make a fine seedbed. I expect about 480 kg per mu if the frost does not bite too hard.

For summer maize, the window after wheat harvest in early June is narrow. I will plant hybrid seed directly into the stubble without ploughing — no-tillage saves my old back and buys me precious days before the rains. I will put down compound fertilizer with the seed and side-dress urea when the plants reach the big trumpet stage, about 15 kg of nitrogen per mu. I will irrigate twice: once at sowing if the soil is dry, and once in July at jointing when the heat is strongest. One good pesticide application for the corn borer and weeds is enough if I watch the fields carefully. I expect around 520 kg per mu.

This is my way. It is not the highest yield in the village, but it is steady, and at my age steady is what keeps us fed.
